answer: The rule is that “The registration of title to every land parcel under this Act shall be in accordance with the cadastral map prepared for that purpose.” Applied here, because the parcel is being brought under the title-registration system, the registration of title must follow the cadastral map prepared for that purpose.

The Commissioner of Title Settlement must, “on receipt of such certified copies of cadastral maps,” publish a “Notice in the Gazette” calling for “any claimants to the land parcel specified in such Notice to submit their claims to him within a prescribed period from the date of publication of such Notice.” [21-1998/section-12]

After claims are received in response to that Notice, the Commissioner of Title Settlement must “cause an investigation to be conducted in order to determine the genuinness or otherwise of claims made in response to a Notice under section 12.” [21-1998/section-13]

The statutory procedures are different:

1. **Reference of disputed claims during investigations**: If, during investigations, the Commissioner of Title Settlement forms the opinion that, because the claims are disputed, it would be more appropriate for the investigations to be carried out by the District Court, the Commissioner **may refer such claims for investigation and determination** to the District Court having jurisdiction over the area where the land is situate. This is a referral made by the Commissioner in the course of the investigation. [21-1998/section-21]

2. **Appeal by an aggrieved claimant**: Any claimant who is aggrieved by a Declaration of the Commissioner of Title Settlement under section 14 **may prefer an appeal against such declaration within the prescribed period** to the District Court having jurisdiction over the area where the land parcel is situate. This is an appeal made by the claimant after the declaration. [21-1998/section-22]

Applied to the facts: because the claims are seriously disputed during the title investigation, the Commissioner may refer those claims to the District Court under section 21. Later, if one claimant is dissatisfied with the Commissioner’s declaration, that claimant’s remedy is to **appeal** to the District Court within the prescribed period under section 22.

The transferee did not acquire the interest. Under s 38, a person acquiring an interest in a land parcel registered under the Act is not entitled to that title or interest unless it is registered under the Act. Under s 39, any transfer or dealing with a registered land parcel or an interest in it must be in accordance with the Act, and every disposition otherwise effected is void. Under s 49, an instrument pertaining to land executed in accordance with the Act “shall take effect on registration” of that instrument under the Act.

Applied here, the instrument was not registered under the Act, so the private agreement alone did not transfer the interest and the transferee did not acquire it. The instrument takes legal effect only on registration.

The statutory rule is that, except in accordance with the provisions of the Act, an instrument pertaining to the ownership of a land parcel registered under the Act, made in favour of two or more persons in common, “shall be void and shall not be registered under this Act.”

Applied to the facts, the registered owner executed one instrument purporting to convey the parcel to two purchasers as owners in common. That is an instrument made in favour of two or more persons in common, so under the provision it is void and not registrable under the Registration of Title Act, unless it is in accordance with some other provision of the Act.

The statutory rule is that, for land or interests in land registered under the Registration of Title Act with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership, the Prescription Ordinance (Chapter 68) “shall not apply,” and the Partition Act also “shall not apply” to land parcels so registered.

Applied to the facts, the parcel is registered with a First Class Title of Absolute Ownership. Therefore, a claim of ownership through prescription cannot rely on the Prescription Ordinance, and a partition action under the Partition Act does not apply to this parcel.

Rule: Under section 59, a Court may order rectification of the Register where it is satisfied that any registration has been obtained by fraud, but the proviso says the Court shall not order rectification so as to affect the title of a registered owner who is in possession and who has acquired the land parcel or interest therein for valuable consideration, unless that owner was a party to the fraud. Under section 60(1)(b), any person suffering loss or damage or who has been prejudiced by reason of “not rectifying the Register in consequence of an order of Court made under section 59” shall, on an order of Court, be entitled to be indemnified by the Government out of the Insurance Fund, unless section 60(2) applies.

Application: Here, the present registered owner is in possession, acquired the parcel for valuable consideration, and was not a party to the fraud. Therefore, the Court may not order rectification so as to affect that owner’s title. The other person who suffered loss because the register was not rectified may claim indemnity under section 60(1)(b), provided the person is not barred by section 60(2) (for example, having caused or substantially contributed to the fraud or deriving title from such a person).

The governing rule is:
- If a person dies intestate leaving a spouse, the surviving spouse inherits one-half of the property. [15-1876/section-22]
- Subject to that spouse’s right, the next order of inheritance is descendants, then ascendants, then collaterals. [15-1876/section-23]
- As between descendants, children, grandchildren, and remoter descendants are preferent; children take equally per capita, but the children or remoter issue of a deceased child take per stirpes, or by representation. [15-1876/section-24]

Application to the facts:
- The surviving spouse takes 1/2 of the estate. [15-1876/section-22]
- The remaining 1/2 goes to descendants. [15-1876/section-23, 15-1876/section-24]
- There are two branches of descendants: (1) the living child, and (2) the branch of the predeceased child, represented by the two grandchildren. Under per stirpes distribution, those two branches share the remaining 1/2 equally.
- So each branch takes 1/2 of the remaining 1/2 = 1/4 of the whole estate.
- The living child therefore receives 1/4.
- The two grandchildren together receive the predeceased child’s 1/4 branch, and because they are the children of that deceased child, they share it equally. Each grandchild receives 1/8.

Final shares:
- Surviving spouse: 1/2
- Living child: 1/4
- Each grandchild: 1/8

Yes. Under Wills Ordinance, s 5, "Every will made beyond the limits of Sri Lanka containing any devise or disposition of immovable property situate within Sri Lanka" is "valid and effectual to alienate and pass the property" if it was "duly made and executed according to and in conformity with the forms and solemnities prescribed by the law of the country where the same shall have been so made and executed," and if it was made by a person who by "the law of such country or of Sri Lanka" was competent to make a will.

Applied here, the will was executed outside Sri Lanka, it disposes of immovable property in Sri Lanka, it complies with the formalities of the country where it was executed, and the testator was competent under that country's law. Those facts satisfy s 5, so the foreign will is capable of validly passing the Sri Lankan immovable property.

Before any precept or order for the service of notice or summons is issued in a proceeding or action for enforcing a right of pre-emption, “proof is furnished to the court of the registration of the proceedings or action as a lis pendens in accordance with the provisions of the Registration of Documents Ordinance.”

As to security for bona fides, the court may, “in its discretion,” order the plaintiff to deposit “the purchase amount set out in the notice given under section 5.”

If the plaintiff defaults in depositing that amount within the period, or any further periods “not exceeding three months in the aggregate,” that the court allows, “his action shall be struck off the roll of pending cases.”

The governing rule is that “A mortgage of a part of a tea or rubber estate as a divided lot shall, if it is effected on or after the appointed day, be null and void notwithstanding anything to the contrary in any other law.”

Applied here, the owner mortgages a physically divided portion of a tea estate as a separate lot after the appointed day. That is a mortgage of part of a tea estate as a divided lot, effected on or after the appointed day. Therefore, the mortgage is null and void.

The rule is that “No share in the common elements of a registered, Condominium Property or of a registered Semi Condominium Property shall be disposed of or otherwise dealt with except as appurtenant to a condominium parcel of such property.” So the share in the common elements cannot be sold or otherwise dealt with separately from the condominium parcel.

The same provision also says that “any alienation of any condominium parcel shall be deemed also to convey the undivided share of the owner in the common elements appertaining to that condominium parcel notwithstanding the fact that no specific or particular reference has been made thereto in the instrument or deed relating to such alienation.” So if the condominium parcel itself is transferred, the attached share in the common elements passes with it automatically, even if the deed does not mention that share.

Applied here, the owner cannot dispose of the share in the common elements separately while retaining the condominium parcel. If the condominium parcel is later transferred, the share in the common elements transfers with the parcel.

The rule is that “The Partition Law shall not apply to any land or building comprised in any registered Condominium Plan.” Applied here, the property is “land and a building already comprised in a registered Condominium Plan,” so the Partition Law does not apply to that property.

Section 13 says that no plan or map, or copy or tracing of a plan or map, is receivable in evidence in any court in Sri Lanka unless it has been prepared in one of the following ways and certified accordingly:

1. it is prepared by or on behalf of the Surveyor-General by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him, and certified by the Surveyor-General or by a registered surveyor duly authorised by him for that purpose; or
2. it is prepared by a registered licensed surveyor and certified by a registered licensed surveyor.

So, a land plan tendered in a civil action is receivable only if it satisfies one of those preparation-and-certification combinations. On the facts given, the plan’s admissibility would depend on whether it was prepared and certified in one of those statutory ways.

Yes. A copy of a cadastral map, plan, or any other plan or map prepared in accordance with any written law, which purports to be a true copy and purports to be signed by the Surveyor-General or any officer acting on his behalf, is “admissible evidence in all cases and for all purposes instead of the original.” It may initially be taken as “prima facie evidence of the truth of the facts stated there in as being that of the original,” and it remains so “until evidence to the contrary shall have first been given.”

No. The statutory rule is that “it shall not be lawful for the company to register a transfer of shares in or debentures of the company, unless a proper instrument of transfer has been delivered to the company.” So, on these facts, where no proper instrument of transfer has been delivered, the company may not register the voluntary transfer.

The exception is that “nothing in this section shall affect any power of the company to register as shareholder or debenture holder, any person to whom the right of any shares in or debentures of the company has been transmitted by operation of law.” So if entitlement to the shares passes by operation of law, the company’s power to register that person is not affected by this section.

Under Companies Act, s 79, a certificate signed under the name of the company by a director and secretary of the company, and specifying shares held by a shareholder, "shall be prima facie evidence of the title of the shareholder to the shares." Applied here, if the certificate is signed in the company's name by a director and the secretary and it specifies the shares held by the person recorded as the shareholder, the certificate has prima facie evidential effect that that person has title to those shares. This means it is evidence of title unless displaced.

The director breached these statutory duties:

1. Under Companies Act, s 188, a director “shall not act or agree to the company acting, in a manner that contravenes any provisions of this Act, or the provisions contained in the articles of the company.” On the facts, the director approved conduct that breaches the company’s articles, so this duty was breached.

2. Under Companies Act, s 189(a), a person exercising powers or performing duties as a director “shall not act in a manner which is reckless or grossly negligent.” On the facts, the director carried out the decision recklessly, so this duty was breached.

3. Under Companies Act, s 189(b), a person exercising powers or performing duties as a director “shall exercise the degree of skill and care that may reasonably be expected of a person of his knowledge and experience.” On the facts, the director did not exercise the skill and care reasonably expected from a person with that director’s knowledge and experience, so this duty was breached.

The Act says that any alienation of land effected in contravention of the Act "shall be void and shall have no effect in law." The Act’s definition of "alienation" includes "transfer" of land. Here, the background says there was a transfer of land completed in direct contravention of the Act, so that transfer is an alienation effected in contravention of the Act and is therefore void and has no effect in law.
